client: I've been a complete mess ever since I messed up my practice presentation yesterday. My mind just went blank halfway through, and now I can't stop thinking about how I'll humiliate myself in front of everyone at the conference next week. I'm not sure talking about it will help - the anxiety feels too real to just talk away.
therapist:
It sounds like that presentation experience really shook your confidence, and now your mind is jumping to worst-case scenarios about the conference. I notice you're speaking very quietly about this - would you say the anxiety feels more overwhelming than the words can capture right now?  

Let's slow down and look at the thoughts driving this distress - what specifically do you fear might happen at the conference?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, it's like... my throat closes up just thinking about it. I keep imagining myself freezing mid-sentence while everyone stares, or someone asking a question I can't answer and the whole room realizing I'm a fraud. 

The worst part is I know these thoughts are irrational, but that doesn't stop my stomach from dropping every time I open the presentation file.
therapist:
Your description of that physical reaction - the throat closing up - tells me this anxiety is hitting you at a very deep level. Even though part of you recognizes these thoughts may be exaggerated, your body is reacting as if the threat is very real.  

When you say you "know" these thoughts are irrational but still feel physically affected, that's an important distinction to notice - would you be willing to explore where that gap between knowing and feeling comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about the gap between knowing and feeling, but that's exactly what frustrates me so much. My logical side knows the anxiety is irrational, but my body reacts like I'm in real danger anyway. It makes me feel like I'm broken or out of control. 

The throat tightening thing happens most when I'm about to speak up in meetings at work. Even when I prepare what to say, my body betrays me like I'm about to face some actual threat instead of just sharing an idea.
therapist:
Your voice sounds different now - more strained and urgent - when describing how your body reacts in meetings. It seems the frustration runs deeper than just the conference presentation.  

That feeling of being "betrayed" by your own body must be so disheartening. Let's unpack this: when your throat tightens in meetings, what's the automatic thought that flashes through your mind in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I always think, "Everyone can see how nervous I am, and they must think I'm incompetent." It makes me feel like I'm losing control of my image at work, which just makes the physical reactions worse. 

Sometimes I wonder if trying to analyze these thoughts just makes me hyper-focus on them more, you know? Like now I'm not just anxious in meetings—I'm anxious about being anxious.
therapist:
I hear how exhausting this cycle feels - worrying about others' perceptions, then worrying about the worry itself. Your voice sounds rushed as you describe this, like your thoughts are racing ahead of you.  

That fear of losing control over how others see you - do you think it might be magnifying the physical reactions, making them feel more threatening than they actually are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, it does feel like everything gets magnified. Like my heart starts racing when I think people are judging me, and then I panic because I'm worried they'll notice how anxious I look. It's this awful loop where I can't tell what's real anymore. 

But I don't know if it's really about control - it's more like I just want to disappear sometimes when I feel this way. The idea that I could change how people see me feels impossible right now.
therapist:
The way you describe wanting to disappear in those moments shows just how overwhelming this feels. I notice your voice sounds higher and tighter when talking about these situations - like the distress is sitting right at the surface.  

When you say you "can't tell what's real anymore" in these moments, can you tell me more about what reality looks like when you're not caught in that anxious loop? What might others actually be seeing when you're in meetings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
When I'm not caught in that anxious spiral, reality is just... normal, I guess? Like, I know logically that people in meetings are probably just focused on their own work, not scrutinizing me. But in the moment, it feels like all eyes are on me, waiting for me to mess up or say something stupid.  

I wish I could hold onto that logical perspective when the anxiety hits, but it's like my brain just won't listen to reason in those moments. It's frustrating because I know how irrational it is, but the fear feels so real.
therapist:
It's interesting how you describe two very different experiences - the logical understanding versus the intense fear in the moment. Your voice sounds more grounded now as you talk about the "normal" reality outside those anxious spikes.  

That gap between knowing and feeling is exactly where we can work - would it help to explore some ways to anchor yourself to that calmer perspective when the anxiety starts rising?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about anchoring myself to the calmer perspective, but in the moment it feels impossible. The anxiety just takes over completely, like my logical thoughts don't even exist anymore. I've tried taking deep breaths before but it never seems to help when I'm really panicking.
therapist:
I hear how defeating it feels when the anxiety seems to erase all your logical thinking in those moments. Your voice sounds a bit more even now as we talk about this, which makes me wonder - have you noticed any situations where the anxiety didn't completely take over, even if just slightly?  

Sometimes small exceptions can show us where the cracks in this pattern might be.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Hmm, I guess there was one time last week when I started feeling anxious about a work deadline, but I managed to send the email anyway. But it still felt awful - my hands were shaking the whole time. I don't know if that really counts as the anxiety not taking over, because I still felt completely overwhelmed by it. 

It's hard for me to see these as "cracks in the pattern" when the anxiety still feels so powerful in those moments. Like even when I push through, it doesn't feel like I'm winning - just surviving.
therapist:
It sounds like even when you push through, the anxiety still colors the whole experience - like you're white-knuckling your way through rather than feeling any sense of mastery. I notice you're speaking quickly about this, with that same urgency we heard earlier when describing the worst moments.  

That distinction between "surviving" versus "winning" is important - what would "winning" look like to you in these situations? Not the absence of anxiety, but maybe having a different relationship with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
Winning... I don't know if I can even imagine that. Right now just getting through the day without panicking feels like an accomplishment. When you ask what winning would look like, part of me thinks that's setting the bar too high - like now I have to "win" at anxiety too? That just makes me feel more pressure. 

But I guess if I really try to picture it... maybe it would be noticing the anxiety but still being able to focus on what I'm doing, instead of the anxiety taking over completely. Though that seems impossible right now.
therapist:
You're speaking more rapidly now as you try to imagine what "winning" could look like - I can hear the struggle in balancing hope with the very real weight of your current experience.  

That small shift you described - noticing the anxiety without it taking over completely - tells me part of you already recognizes this isn't about eliminating anxiety, but changing how you respond to it. Would it help if we explored that idea more, at a pace that doesn't add pressure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I do want to believe change is possible, but part of me keeps thinking "what if this is just how I am?" The anxiety feels so heavy sometimes, like it's built into me. When you say "changing how I respond," I get stuck because my first instinct is always panic - how do I even start rewiring that?
therapist:
I hear that weariness in your voice as you wonder if this anxiety might just be "how you are" - it makes sense to feel that way when these patterns have been so persistent. That quiet, hesitant way you're speaking tells me how heavy this doubt feels right now.  

You're absolutely right that we can't erase that first instinct of panic - but what if we viewed it like building a muscle? Not about eliminating the initial reaction, but gradually strengthening your ability to respond differently afterward. Would exploring small, manageable steps in that direction feel overwhelming right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
